sysd-scale-057.title: Performance bottleneck: the slowest part sets the pace
sysd-scale-057.text: A system moves at the speed of its slowest part. A bottleneck occurs when the capacity of an application or computer system is limited by a single component. It is the part with the lowest throughput of all parts of the transaction path. A common example is code that could use parallel processing but runs several independent processes sequentially instead of simultaneously. Tracking down bottlenecks, or hot spots, is called performance analysis. It is done with specialized profilers, with the objective of making those sections of code as fast as possible. Bottlenecks, like series circuits, are design structures that create single points of failure.

sysd-scale-048.title: Replication lag: reading your own writes
sysd-scale-048.text: You place an order, check your order list a moment later, and the order is missing. The likely culprit is replication lag, the delay in propagating changes from the leader to its replicas, which can leave replicas serving stale data. Under network delay or server overload, replica data might be seconds or even minutes behind the primary. A user who checks an order right after placing it may hit a lagging replica and not see the order at all, so the setup needs read-after-write consistency. One mitigation is to send latency-sensitive reads, and reads that immediately follow writes, to the primary database. Another is to check whether a replica has caught up with the primary, which a relational database generally supports. Query the replica if it is up to date. Otherwise fail the read or read from the primary.

sysd-scale-050.title: Active and passive replication: who does the work?
sysd-scale-050.text: When a request arrives, who does the work: every replica, or just one? In the active form, every replica processes the same request. In the passive form, one replica processes each request and transfers the result to the others. In a primary-backup or primary-replica scheme, one leader replica chosen by leader election processes all requests, a design predominant in high-availability clusters. In a multi-primary or multi-master scheme, any replica can process a request and distribute the new state. That calls for some form of distributed concurrency control, such as a {{ref:sysd-scale-007}} manager. {{ref:sysd-scale-020}} is sometimes mistakenly used as a synonym of {{ref:sysd-scale-106}}.

sysd-scale-052.title: Chain replication: writes that travel down a line
sysd-scale-052.text: In chain replication, a write must pass through several nodes one after another. It is a family of multi-primary protocols that arrange replicas in a chain for writes to get high throughput and strong consistency. Modern multi-primary replication protocols optimize for the common failure-free operation, and chain replication is a popular family of them. It enables local reads on all replica nodes but has high latency for writes, which must traverse several nodes sequentially. The Hermes protocol takes another route. It combines invalidations and logical timestamps for strong consistency with local reads and high-performance writes from all replicas, committing after one multicast round trip.

sysd-scale-053.title: Three ways to ship changes to a replica
sysd-scale-053.text: A leader can describe its changes to replicas in three ways. Statement-based replication logs write requests such as SQL statements and sends them to replicas for execution, which is problematic with non-deterministic functions or statements with side effects. Write-ahead log shipping replicates the storage engine's low-level log, which keeps data structures identical across nodes. Logical (row-based) replication describes changes at the row level in a dedicated log format, giving more flexibility and independence from storage engine internals.

sysd-scale-132.title: Logical replication: publishing changes row by row
sysd-scale-132.text: Not every copy has to be a byte-for-byte clone. Logical replication replicates data objects and their changes based on their replication identity, usually a primary key, rather than copying physical blocks. Physical replication, which PostgreSQL also supports, uses exact block addresses and byte-by-byte copying. Logical replication uses a publish and subscribe model. Subscribers pull data from the publications they subscribe to on a publisher node, and may re-publish it to allow cascading or more complex setups. Replication of a table starts with a snapshot copy to the subscriber. Changes made since the copy are then sent continually and applied in the publisher's order, so transactional consistency holds within one subscription. Use cases include sending a subset of a database's changes, consolidating databases for analytics, replicating between major versions or platforms, and sharing a subset of data. A read-only subscriber causes no conflicts from a single subscription, but other writes to the same tables can cause conflicts.

sysd-scale-051.title: Three models of replication
sysd-scale-051.text: Three models of data replication are widely cited. Transactional replication, used for replicating transactional data such as a database, follows one-copy serializability: valid outcomes on replicated data accord with ACID. The second model, {{ref:sysd-scale-020}}, assumes a deterministic finite automaton and {{ref:sysd-scale-113}} of every event. It is based on {{ref:sysd-scale-008}} and is usually implemented as a replicated log of {{ref:sysd-scale-015}} rounds. In virtual synchrony, processes form a group, and a joining process receives a checkpoint of the replicated state. Multicasts reach all members in identical order, with membership changes delivered as a new membership view.

sysd-scale-054.title: Storage replication: copying disks, not files
sysd-scale-054.text: Copy the disk and everything on it is copied too. Storage replication copies block-device updates to several physical disks, so any file system on top is replicated without modification. It is implemented in a disk array controller or in a device driver. Disk mirroring is the most basic method, but replication can also cross a network to distant disks. The purpose is to prevent damage from failures or disasters at one location or to improve the ability to recover data. Point-in-time replication copies periodic snapshots of only the changed data, so it can use cheaper links such as iSCSI or T1 instead of fiberoptic lines.

sysd-scale-130.title: Choosing a replication solution
sysd-scale-130.text: No single replication solution fits every workload. Database servers can work together in two ways. For high availability, a second server takes over if the primary fails. For load balancing, several computers serve the same data. Read-only servers combine easily, but read/write servers are hard, because a write to any server must reach all servers so later reads stay consistent. This synchronization problem is the fundamental difficulty, and each solution minimizes it for a specific workload. Some let only one server modify data: a warm standby cannot be connected to until promoted, while a hot standby accepts read-only queries. Functionality is traded against performance.

sysd-scale-055.title: File-based replication: copying files, not blocks
sysd-scale-055.text: Instead of a whole 4,096-byte disk block, file-level replication can transmit just the 100 bytes an application wrote. File-based replication copies data at the logical level of individual files rather than at the storage block level. It relies almost exclusively on software. A kernel filter driver can intercept file system calls such as open, write and delete and send them to another machine, which mimics them. It can skip data of no business value, such as temporary files. Batch replication compares source and destination and makes the destination match. It is generally free or inexpensive, such as rsync, but system-intensive, so it generally runs infrequently.

sysd-scale-123.title: Split-brain: two nodes that both think they are in charge
sysd-scale-123.text: High-availability clusters watch node health over a private heartbeat link. If all those links fail while the nodes keep running, each node believes it is the only one running. That is split-brain: a state of data or availability inconsistency caused by two separate data sets with overlapping scope. It typically arises when servers stop communicating and synchronizing, as in a {{ref:sysd-scale-142}}. Each side then serves clients from its own data set with no coordination, which can corrupt data. The SRE book's diagnosis is that such a system solves a leader election problem with simple timeouts. But leader election is a form of distributed {{ref:sysd-scale-008}} and cannot be solved correctly using heartbeats. Optimistic approaches let partitioned nodes keep working, gaining availability at the cost of correctness. Pessimistic approaches give up availability for consistency by limiting access to sub-partitions. The typical pessimistic approach is a quorum vote: the sub-partition with a majority of the votes stays available and the others fence themselves off. A two-node cluster without a witness cannot tell which member should be active when the heartbeat fails.

sysd-scale-126.title: Sending state or sending operations: two kinds of CRDT
sysd-scale-126.text: State-based CRDTs replicate by sending full state to be merged, while operation-based CRDTs replicate by sending the update operations. State-based ones (CvRDTs) send their full local state, and the merge must be commutative, associative and idempotent, so reordering and duplicated messages do no harm. They are simpler to design and need only a gossip protocol, but the whole state must eventually reach every replica. Operation-based ones (CmRDTs) send operations such as +10 or -20, which must be commutative and associative. They use less bandwidth when transactions are few compared with the state size, but need middleware that never drops or duplicates operations and delivers them in causal order.

sysd-scale-127.title: Counters and sets built as CRDTs
sysd-scale-127.text: A counter that many machines update at once needs a slot per machine. A G-Counter gives each node an array slot to increment. Replicas merge by taking the maximum of every slot, and the value is the sum of the slots. A PN-Counter combines two G-Counters, one for increments and one for decrements, and its value is the increment total minus the decrement total. A G-Set only allows adds and merges by union, and a 2P-Set adds a tombstone set so elements can be removed, though a removed element can never return. An OR-Set tags each add uniquely and removes only the tags it has observed.

reviews.replication: Replication keeps several copies of data so that no single part can stop the system, and failover lets a standby or replica take over when a copy fails. Single-leader designs send every write to one node, which makes consistency easier to achieve, while multi-master and leaderless designs accept writes anywhere and must resolve conflicts, sometimes with CRDTs. Synchronous replication waits for the remote copy and loses nothing, while asynchronous replication runs faster but can lose recent data and serve stale reads. Quorums and leader election keep copies in agreement, and split-brain shows what happens when they fail. Replicas can be fed by logs, rows, blocks or files, so the right solution depends on the workload.
